Safety screen: all 13 are legitimate public places (a park, a memorial square, a lakeside garden, a wetland trail, a library, a museum, an art centre, two cafes, a heritage courtyard, a church, a beach park, a beach); none involve trespass, derelict, industrial or rail land. The skeptic reread every safety note against the standard and found none that characterised people or leaned on a neighbourhood's reputation; all rest on lighting, closing times, traffic, water and terrain. Caution is set on the two beaches only, for currents and unlit sand after dark.

spots.name: Viharamahadevi Park
spots.blurb: Colombo's oldest and largest park, a rectangle of rain trees, flowering mara and lawns between the Town Hall and the National Museum. Office workers eat lunch under the trees, couples sit on the benches around the giant seated Buddha, and the shaded paths on the museum side are quiet even when the fountain end is busy. It is the default answer when a resident wants somewhere green to sit for an hour in the middle of the city.
spots.tips: Enter from the Town Hall side (Green Path) or from Sir Marcus Fernando Mawatha by the museum; the south-western corner and the paths near the Public Library are quietest. Early morning is walkers and joggers, late afternoon is families. Carry water, there is little for sale inside.

safety.note: Open, well-used park bordered by busy roads with lit main paths; the interior paths are dim after sunset, so stay near the Town Hall or museum edges once it is dark.

spots.verifyNote: Well-known public monument and grounds, written from knowledge; no search spent. Wikipedia title from knowledge, not URL-confirmed. Coordinates are for the memorial hall itself.
spots.name: Independence Square
spots.blurb: The stone-pillared Independence Memorial Hall sits in a wide, lawned square that Colombo treats as its evening living room: walkers do laps of the perimeter path, students sit on the steps under the carved lions, and the whole thing is lit until late. The old Auditor General's building beside it is now the Arcade, a quiet colonial courtyard with cafes if you want a table. Weekday mornings before 8am are almost empty.
spots.tips: Sit on the raised steps of the hall itself for shade and a breeze, or on the lawn edges facing the Arcade. Go before 7am for joggers-only quiet, or after 8pm when the lights are on and the heat is gone. Toilets and coffee are in the Arcade next door.

safety.note: Floodlit, busy with walkers until around 10pm and patrolled; the surrounding roads carry fast traffic, so use the crossings at Independence Avenue.

spots.name: Diyatha Uyana
spots.blurb: A lakeside park on the banks of the Diyawanna Oya, a few kilometres east of the centre near Parliament, built on reclaimed marsh with a long waterside walkway, a plant and flower market, food stalls and a small aquarium. It is where suburban Colombo comes on weekend evenings to walk by the water and eat, and on weekday afternoons the lakefront benches are mostly empty. The view west over the water at sunset is one of the widest open horizons the city has.
spots.tips: Take the bus or a tuk to Polduwa junction and walk in from Parliament Road; head past the stalls to the waterside path for benches facing the lake. Weekends fill up after 4pm with families; go on a weekday afternoon for quiet. The floating restaurant next door is separate and pricier.

sources.label: Tripadvisor: Diyatha Uyana at Polduwa junction

safety.note: Lit, staffed park busy into the evening; the lake edge is low and unfenced in places, so keep to the paved walkway with children.

spots.name: Beddagana Wetland Park
spots.blurb: A boardwalk and dirt-path loop through a stretch of the Diyawanna wetland behind the old Kotte ramparts, with bird hides, a small observation tower and a lot of herons, kingfishers and water monitors. It was built as an urban wetland reserve rather than a leisure park, so there are no stalls and no crowds, only the odd birder and a few neighbours walking. Sitting in a hide for an hour with the city noise gone is as close to countryside as Colombo gets without leaving it.
spots.tips: Small entry fee at the gate; bring water, a hat and insect repellent, and go before 9am for birds and shade. Boardwalks are the main route, and the tower at the far end has the best view over the reed beds. Last entry is 5:30pm and the gate closes at 6pm.

safety.note: Gated and ticketed, closes at 6pm; paths are unlit and can be muddy after rain, and the water is unfenced, so stay on the boardwalks and keep back from the lake edge.

spots.name: Colombo Public Library
spots.blurb: The city's main public library, a 1980s concrete building set in trees on the edge of Viharamahadevi Park, with big reading rooms, a periodicals section and ceiling fans. Students and retirees fill the desks on weekday afternoons, and it is one of the few places in central Colombo where you can sit for hours in the cool, out of the rain, without buying anything. The park is right outside for when you want to move.
spots.tips: Bring ID; membership is only needed to borrow, and reading rooms are open to walk-ins (a token charge may apply, check at the desk). Upstairs reading rooms are quieter than the ground floor. Bags may need to be left at the counter. Closed on public holidays.

safety.note: Staffed public building with security at the door; the walk back through the park edge is dim after dark, so use the Sir Marcus Fernando Mawatha side.

spots.name: Colombo National Museum
spots.blurb: A white Italianate colonial building of 1877 set in its own lawns beside Viharamahadevi Park, with long, high-ceilinged galleries of Kandyan regalia, stone Buddhas, palm-leaf manuscripts and colonial furniture. It is rarely crowded outside school-trip mornings, the upstairs galleries are cool and echoing, and the wide verandahs and lawn benches are a good place to sit even if you skip the collection. It is more a rainy-afternoon refuge than a blockbuster.
spots.tips: Buy a ticket at the gate (foreigners pay more than residents); leave big bags at the cloakroom. Head upstairs first for the quietest rooms, then sit on the front verandah looking out over the lawns. Closed on public holidays and some Poya days, so check before going.

safety.note: Staffed, ticketed building with guards in the galleries; the grounds close with the museum at 5pm.

spots.name: Lionel Wendt Art Centre
spots.blurb: Colombo's oldest working arts venue, opened in 1953 on the site of photographer Lionel Wendt's house, with a theatre and two free galleries that show a rolling programme of local painters and photographers. The ground-floor gallery is almost always empty on a weekday afternoon, and the shaded garden and steps outside are where the city's artists and theatre people drink tea between shows. It is the kind of place a resident sends a friend rather than a tour group.
spots.tips: Galleries are free and usually open daytime, but they close between exhibitions, so check the lionelwendt.org listings first. Evenings bring theatre crowds; the garden benches are the quiet spot. It sits a short walk from the National Museum and the park.
spots.hours: varies (galleries roughly 10am-6pm when a show is on; check site)

safety.note: Staffed venue on a quiet residential street; lit at the entrance on show nights, dim otherwise, so book a ride home from the door after evening performances.

spots.name: Barefoot Garden Cafe
spots.blurb: The courtyard cafe behind Barefoot, the handloom textile shop that has been on Galle Road since the 1960s: a shaded garden of frangipani and tables under a canopy, reached through the shop and its small bookshop and gallery. The traffic noise of Galle Road disappears completely once you are in the back, and it has long been where Colombo's writers and NGO workers spend a slow afternoon with a pot of tea and a book. Sunday afternoons sometimes have live jazz.
spots.tips: Walk through the shop to the garden; the tables furthest from the kitchen are quietest. Go on a weekday mid-afternoon for space, and browse the bookshop and upstairs gallery on the way out. Closes at 7pm (6pm Sundays and Poya days), so it is a daytime place.

safety.note: Staffed, enclosed garden; the only hazard is crossing Galle Road outside, which is fast and has few signalled crossings, so use the one at Kollupitiya junction.

spots.name: Pagoda Tea Room
spots.blurb: A tea room that has been serving Fort's office workers since 1884, in an old building on Chatham Street with wooden tables, ceiling fans and a counter of short eats, fish buns and cakes. It is unfussy, cheap and unchanged, and between the breakfast and lunch rushes you can sit with a pot of Ceylon tea for as long as you like while the street outside goes about its business. Locals know it as the place Duran Duran filmed in the 1980s; nobody else notices.
spots.tips: Order at the counter; the breakfast run before 9am is the busiest, so 10am-noon or 2-4pm is the quiet window. It closes at 5:30pm and all day Sunday, when Fort itself is shuttered and empty. Pair it with a walk down Chatham Street to the Clock Tower and the Dutch Hospital.

safety.note: Staffed cafe on a busy commercial street in daylight; Fort empties out after offices close and some streets near the President's House are subject to security checkpoints, so carry ID.

spots.verifyNote: Well-known heritage precinct, written from knowledge; no search spent. Wikipedia title from knowledge, not URL-confirmed. Courtyards are freely accessible; the cafes are commercial.
spots.name: Old Colombo Dutch Hospital
spots.blurb: A 17th-century Dutch hospital with two long courtyards under tiled roofs and deep verandahs, restored in 2011 as a precinct of cafes and shops opposite the World Trade Center. The courtyards themselves are open to anyone, the arcades keep off both sun and rain, and the benches in the inner courtyard are a calm place to sit while Fort's office crowd comes and goes. Late evening, when the shops shut and the restaurants thin out, it is quiet and lit.
spots.tips: Come in from Hospital Street or Bank of Ceylon Mawatha; the inner (eastern) courtyard is the quieter of the two. You can sit on the benches without buying anything. Sunday daytime, when the rest of Fort is closed, is unexpectedly peaceful.
spots.hours: courtyards open roughly 10am-midnight (shops and cafes vary)

safety.note: Lit, staffed precinct with security at the entrances until the restaurants close; the streets around it are quiet and dim late at night, so book a ride from the courtyard.

spots.verifyNote: Historic church, written from knowledge; no search spent. Wikipedia title from knowledge, not URL-confirmed. Coordinates are my estimate of the church on its hill in Pettah and could be 100-200 m off. Visiting hours outside Sunday services depend on the caretaker.
spots.name: Wolvendaal Church
spots.blurb: A Dutch Reformed church of 1749 on a low hill above the market streets of Pettah, thick-walled and cross-shaped, its floor paved with the tombstones of Dutch governors. Inside it is dim, cool and utterly silent while the bazaar roars two streets away; outside, the walled churchyard has benches and shade. It is one of the few places in Pettah where you can sit down at all, and almost nobody visits.
spots.tips: Climb Wolvendaal Street from the Main Street end; a caretaker usually opens the doors on weekday daytimes and a small donation is welcome. Sunday morning services are in Sinhala, Tamil and English. Combine it with a wander through the Pettah markets before or after, they are best before noon.
spots.hours: varies (usually daytime when the caretaker is present; Sunday services)

safety.note: Walled churchyard with a caretaker in daylight; the approach streets are narrow, crowded with handcarts and traffic, and the church is closed after dark, so this is a daytime visit.

spots.name: Crow Island Beach Park
spots.blurb: A 17-acre beach park at the northern tip of the city, where the Kelani River meets the sea, with a long paved walkway along the sand, a small lake, mangroves and a kite-flying lawn. It was rebuilt as a public park in 2016 and is used almost entirely by the surrounding neighbourhoods: evening walkers, kids on bikes, families on the grass. The sunset over the open sea with container ships queuing for the port is as good as Galle Face and a fraction as busy.
spots.tips: Take a tuk or the bus up to Mattakkuliya; the walkway runs the length of the beach and the benches nearest the river mouth are quietest. Weekday late afternoon is best. Swimming is not advised here, sit and watch instead. Bring water, the stalls are intermittent.

safety.note: Strong currents where the river meets the sea and no lifeguards, so do not swim; the walkway is lit but the sand and mangrove paths are not, and the park is a long way from the centre, so leave by dusk and arrange your ride back in advance.

spots.name: Mount Lavinia Beach
spots.blurb: Colombo's local beach, a long curve of golden sand about 10 km south of the centre, reached by the coastal railway in twenty minutes. The stretch north of the old hotel headland, along College Avenue, is lined with simple seafood shacks and a few smarter restaurants where you can sit at a table on the sand with a king coconut and watch the sun go down; further north toward Dehiwala the beach is just sand, fishing boats and dog-walkers. Residents come on weekend evenings, and on weekday mornings it is nearly empty.
spots.tips: Take the train to Mount Lavinia station, walk down Hotel Road toward the hotel and turn right onto College Avenue; the lanes between the restaurants lead onto the sand. The shacks nearest the headland are busiest, so walk five minutes north for quiet. The sea is rough with strong currents, so paddle rather than swim. Sunset is about 6-6:30pm year round.

safety.note: No lifeguards and a strong undertow year round, so stay in the shallows; the restaurant-lined stretch north of the hotel is lit until late but the sand beyond it is dark, so keep to the lit section after sunset and plan the ride or train back.
